asr_transcript: The star-forming main sequence links stellar mass to how quickly stars form. The mass-metallicity relation links stellar mass to oxygen abundance. This study asks how both changed toward the early universe. About 490,000 Sloan Digital Sky Survey galaxies set the nearby baseline. 180 James Webb spectroscopic galaxies provide early star formation. 145 also provide metallicity. Another 3,743 infrared catalog sources add only star formation statistics because they lack metallicity. A calibration turns spectral lines into oxygen abundance. The authors rebuild the nearby benchmark with 200,000 SDSS galaxies on an electron temperature anchored scale, matching the early sample. Then every early galaxy is compared at the same stellar mass. A DEX is logarithmic. At fixed mass, star formation is 0.77 DEX above nearby galaxies at Redshift 3.5, about six times faster. At Redshift 6.7, 1.94 DEX means nearly 90 times faster. The last bin has 46 galaxies above Redshift 6. This James Webb sample favors strong emission lines and unusually intense star formation for each mass. So the reported elevation may be inflated and should be read cautiously. Oxygen deficits are 0.43, 0.37, and 0.40 DEX at Redshift's 4.6, 5.3, and 7.2. Each corresponds to about 40% of nearby oxygen abundance at fixed mass. From Redshift 4 to 7, the median metallicity deficit stays nearly flat. Yet the middle 68% spans 0.5 DEX, about a factor of three, and some galaxies lie within 0.15 DEX of the nearby relation. The sample is diverse. Roughly 0.1 DEX of calibration uncertainty remains and the low mass nearby relation is extrapolated. Emission line selection matters. This machine-generated manuscript uses public queries. Its status is descriptive and not validated. Automated review is not journal or human peer review.
